## About the module

Developed by Tao Wen for the IAMG 2026 short course, this guided exercise uses river chemistry to distinguish carbonate-dominated catchments from those dominated by crystalline silicate rocks. Learners compare a linear classifier with a small neural network in PyTorch.

- **Audience:** Geoscientists with basic Python skills; no prior PyTorch, deep-learning, or hydrogeochemistry experience required.
- **Estimated time:** 40–45 minutes.
- **Tools:** Google Colab on a free CPU runtime; no GPU or manual data upload required. Local Jupyter instructions are also available.
- **Developer:** Tao Wen, Syracuse University.
- **Teaching data:** A curated GLORICH subset with nine chemistry inputs for 2,986 stations.

[Open the guided notebook in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/jaywt/iamg-2026-dl-geochemistry/blob/main/notebooks/glorich_lithology_pytorch.ipynb){.btn .btn-primary}

[View the module repository](https://github.com/jaywt/iamg-2026-dl-geochemistry) · [Read the instructor guide](https://github.com/jaywt/iamg-2026-dl-geochemistry/blob/main/INSTRUCTOR_GUIDE.md)

## Learning goals

- Define predictors and target classes from a geoscience question.
- Split data before fitting transformations, then train and compare models.
- Evaluate class imbalance and interpret classification metrics.
- Experiment with activation functions and discuss limits of geographic transfer.

A random station split tests performance in similar sampled settings. It does not establish transfer to unfamiliar regions or prove that lithology alone controls river chemistry.
